title: Explicit Instruction in an Implicit World: Learning to Teach, Teaching to Learn
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood opens with the Scarecrow and the Wizard's diploma as an image of the straw man, then argues that the explicit versus implicit instruction debate rests on one. In his view all teaching is explicit to varying degrees, and the narrower sense now promoted in state and federal documents as direct instruction is really a commercial, scripted product. He sets out the mainstream explicit model of objectives, modelling, checking and guided practice, credits its value for technical skills, and shows how a lesson can be designed in either mode using his ABCD planning acronym. He argues that guided practice and the more open work of building thinking require skilled implicit moves designed explicitly. His main objection is that scripts deskill teachers, taking over the teacher's voice and mind at the moment of learning, and he cites the 2008 Education Science rejection of the evidence for DI materials. He closes by rejecting the dichotomy and scripted lessons while affirming lesson design as core professional competence.
points: The explicit versus implicit dichotomy is a straw man, because deliberate teaching is explicit to varying degrees and good guided practice depends on implicit moves.
Explicit instruction in the Madeline Hunter tradition suits technical micro skills and content knowledge, but its rigidity tends to increase in high-poverty schools.
The ABCD lesson design frame of audience, behavior, content and delivery shows the same objective can be taught in more explicit or more inferential modes.
Scripted direct instruction aims to take design work and cognitive load away from teachers, which Underwood calls deskilling that appropriates the teacher's voice during learning.
Implicit learning in the psychological sense is too theoretically fluid for schools to rely on for higher-order intellectual growth.
quotes: In some discourse settings the debate has been framed around the dichotomy of explicit vs implicit instruction. In my view, there is no dichotomy: All teaching is explicit in varying degrees.

Explicit instruction as I’ve come to see it working with my colleagues in a Reading Specialist credential program is an umbrella concept with a core sense of “clear, unmistakable, designed to stimulate learning.” Seen in this light, pedagogy of all sorts is a deliberate, coherent public act undertaken on behalf of a child designed to foster more complex competence and understanding.

In my experience implicit instruction is the more difficult part in planning and executing explicit instruction in regular classrooms. Guided practice in particular requires a skillful teacher with highly developed levels of relational thinking and alertness to social moves.
Explicit instruction is the dominant tradition in American public schools. In many ways it provided the engine that made the factory we still have today academically productive, such as it has been.

The aim as near as I can see is to relieve teachers from the burden of designing instruction, to provide lessons that are inherently better (e.g., more systematic), or to lessen the cognitive load on teachers and place it in the hands of commercial publishers. In its most extreme forms, DI appropriates the teacher’s voice and mind at the time they need it most—during acts of learning.

I’ve done my best to fairly represent current notions of explicit instruction and direct instruction using documents prepared by proponents available in the public domain. I reject the explicit vs implicit dichotomy. I reject scripted lessons as dangerously distorted instruction.

It has been called “unintentional” or “incidental” or “unconscious” or “unaware” learning because the learner was not formally “taught” and did not set out to learn. I’m not well versed in the psychological research, but as near as I can tell, schools would likely not do well to count on it for higher-order intellectual growth.
